The post Leading universities when the old rules no longer quite apply appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
For those attending this year’s party conferences, join HEPI for our 2026 Party Conference ringe events, at the Labour Party Conference on Monday 28 September in Liverpool and the Conservative Party Conference on Monday 5 October in Birmingham.

At both conferences, HEPI will host two events exploring some of the biggest issues facing higher education:

Higher Education Question Time, bringing together sector leaders to answer your questions about the key challenges and opportunities for universities,

Soft power in a hardening world: is the UK making the most of its global assets?, examining the UK’s international influence and the role of higher education within it.

All events take place outside the secure zones, so no conference pass is required. Register your interest now. As with all party conference fringe events, attendance is first come, first served and registering does not guarantee you will get a seat.

This blog was kindly authored by Ben Tucker, Partner at Minerva.

There has probably never been a harder time to be leading a university. That is not a plea for sympathy. The vice-chancellors, principals and presidents we interviewed for our recent report (Leading in Times of Turmoil) were not self-pitying, nor cynical, nor seeking to present themselves as heroic figures standing alone against the storm. If anything, what came through most strongly was sobriety: a deep commitment to their institutions and to higher education, combined with a very clear-eyed sense that the job has changed.

For the past few years, the sector has been menaced by a many-headed beast: funding shortfalls; volatility in international recruitment; regulatory and political pressure; pensions; energy costs; AI; changing student behaviours; culture wars; and repeated restructuring. What is striking is not simply that these pressures exist, but the speed with which leaders now have to respond.

“The timing has become much more compressed.”

In this context, the first task of leadership is not frantic activity, but clarity. Again and again, interviewees returned to the importance of knowing what sort of university they serve. In easier times, institutional mission statements can feel ornamental. In harder times, they become practical: helping leaders decide what to stop doing, where to invest, what kind of growth is worth pursuing, and what must be protected.

One of the report’s clearest themes is that

“crisis management is not the same as strategic leadership.”

Universities do need to address deficits, reduce costs and improve productivity. But if everything becomes only a financial exercise, institutions risk losing the very qualities that make them universities. The best leaders use strategy as both a rallying call and a discipline.

The second task is more prosaic, but just as important: running the business. There is now no plausible version of the vice-chancellor role that allows someone to stand apart from the finances. “Business-like” is sometimes used pejoratively in higher education, but the leaders we spoke to were not trying to make universities less human. They were trying to ensure that they survive.

This is also why team-building matters so much. Vice-chancellors are not, and should not be, solitary problem-solvers. Many described the work of building executive teams that can operate across institutional siloes, challenge each other honestly, and own shared problems. Leaner teams only work if they are more trusted, more candid and more focused.

Communication has changed too. A few years ago, discussions of university leadership often circled around authenticity and personality. In the present moment, the tone feels different. Leaders need to front things up: to stand in rooms, answer questions, explain the burning platform without theatricality, and offer enough hope to keep people moving.

But the most important focus at the moment may be governance. Governance is no longer a periodic process that sits politely alongside executive leadership; it has become one of the central conditions for whether leadership succeeds. As one interviewee observed,

“Governance has changed a lot. Board members can no longer turn up, eat sandwiches and go to a graduation.”

This matters because the increasing business dimension of a vice-chancellor’s life is paralleled by an increasing need for business-like governance. Leaders talked about absolute openness with boards, regular contact with chairs, informal conversations and the discipline of “no nasty surprises”. One described spending 10–15 per cent of each week on board work. The board relationship is not peripheral to effectiveness; it is increasingly part of the job itself.

This does not mean boards becoming executive teams by another name. The challenge is subtler: to govern in the realm of what is possible. Lay members can bring immense value, but they are necessarily at some distance from the lived realities of the institution. In difficult times, that distance can become dangerous if boards ask impossible levels of performance from exhausted organisations. One leader captured the problem bluntly:

“Stop asking for the moon when you know we can’t deliver it.”

For those appointing leaders, this has real implications. Governance can be one of the biggest shocks for people arriving in vice-chancellor roles: suddenly they become the singular focus of intense board attention. Candidates need business understanding, strategic clarity, resilience and humility, but they also need to know how to build trust with a chair, work constructively with lay members, and keep a board close without allowing it to drift into operational management. Boards, in turn, should invest more consciously in board culture, chair development, realistic performance expectations and induction for new vice-chancellors.

There is no single model that will work for every institution. Higher education is becoming more multiple, not less. Different universities face different combinations of challenge and opportunity. Some will become more specialised; some will collaborate more radically; some may merge where there is no better alternative. The task is not to pretend that one sector-wide answer exists, but to steward institutional distinctiveness intelligently.

These are not tranquil times, and they are unlikely to become tranquil soon. But turmoil can clarify as well as threaten. If universities can use this moment to become sharper about purpose, more honest about performance, more open in governance and more thoughtful about leadership, then the sector may emerge not unscathed, but stronger in the places that matter.

title: Career focus and a community campus: how the University of Birmingham got its mojo back

The Covid pandemic upended almost every corner of British life, and universities were no exception. But for the University of Birmingham, the turmoil became a turning point.

The pandemic made the university think long and hard about the type of education it was delivering for its students, says Deborah Longworth, Birmingham’s pro-vice-chancellor for education. This sparked an overhaul of its teaching and curriculum – which has been rewarded with impressive results.

This year the University of Birmingham has been ranked in the Guardian University Guide’s top 20 for the first time in nearly a decade, reaching its highest ever position of 14th overall. The improvement is mainly thanks to a strong recovery in Birmingham students’ views of the university, after it dipped to alarmingly low levels during the pandemic and its aftermath.

Before 2020, Birmingham prided itself on providing a good experience on campus. “Covid really hit that, of course,” Longworth says. “But I don’t think we’d caught up with the things that really concerned and worried students, and what it was that they were most interested in … I think that got more exposed when we didn’t have students on campus.”

That began a university-wide programme of change, starting with the teaching timetable and including new elements woven into the undergraduate curriculum to enhance academic skills and help students secure a career of their choosing.

For first-year undergraduates that includes courses on how to develop a LinkedIn profile – something that can come as a shock to parents who graduated from university at a time when many courses were unconcerned with career prospects.

Adam Tickell, who took over as Birmingham’s vice-chancellor in 2022 as it was emerging from the pandemic, said the emphasis on developing employable skills within academic courses reflects the social change in the numbers going into higher education.

“It’s partly a recognition that so many more young people go to university than when I did. I graduated in the 1980s and one in 10 people went to university then, and now it’s around one in four, one in three. So things are different,” Tickell says.

“But it’s partly because even if your career aspiration is to get a job in creative arts or [if you’re] doing an English degree and want to work in publishing – how can we equip those students for the jobs they want?

“That’s not the same as saying we’re equipping them for jobs they don’t want to do and they just have to be motivated. We know that motivations can vary. Ultimately graduates do want control over their careers, so we’re trying to equip them for the job they really want rather than anything else.”

So far the results have been impressive: nearly nine out of 10 recent graduates would choose to study at Birmingham again, according to data from the Higher Education Statistics Agency.

The university is also adding an innovative programme named Ad Alta – taken from its Latin motto meaning striving for excellence – to explicitly develop students’ skills as part of the curriculum, as well a novel option that allows undergraduates to take an extra year to study an unrelated subject, such as AI and data science or environmental sustainability, outside their existing courses.

Matt Hiely-Rayner, who compiles the Guardian’s University Guide, says Birmingham’s performance had been handicapped in recent years by below-average levels of student satisfaction, as measured by the Office for Students’ annual national student survey (NSS), especially in core disciplines such as medicine.

But the negative effects it recorded after the pandemic, which saw it drop to 37th overall four years ago, have now fallen away.

“Generally the results from the NSS are the biggest change for Birmingham. In the past it may have been doing less well but its results have improved a great deal, and very rapidly,” says Hiely-Rayner, who noted that Birmingham’s highlights include top five places in a broad range of subjects including computer science, physics, music and drama and dance.

Meanwhile Birmingham’s international reputation has also improved. In this year’s prestigious QS world university rankings, which are largely based on quality of research output, Birmingham has climbed to 68th in the world alongside the University of Warwick

The improvements in student satisfaction have come after the university’s leadership invested in encouraging students to provide feedback, and then responding to it.

“We set a very clear and persistent message that student experience in the round is the whole institution’s job. Every professional service unit, every academic unit, whether you’re the head of college or the head of a school, it’s everyone’s job. We gave ourselves really clear targets. We said this is not good enough. We need to do better for our students,” Longworth says.

“Students probably felt we were over-asking them for feedback. But then if they gave us some, we answered it.”

Other major changes were aimed at overhauling teaching quality and assessment, starting with reorganising the university’s calendar.

“We moved away from the semester system, which I think had been a challenge for us. The curriculum couldn’t breathe in the semester system. We had piled on assessment, lots of smaller assessments, and I think that had put a lot of pressure on students. So we gave them some more time by going back to the three-term system.”

The changes created space for Ad Alta, which Longworth calls “the core of all our undergraduate degrees”. It was developed with employer and graduate input and is designed to foster the qualities that students will need for their future careers.

The first 2,000 undergraduates started the Ad Alta programmes last year (2025-26), developing academic study skills, to be followed in their second year by working on challenges for external employers or community organisations, finishing with a research essay or design project and culminating in an additional “Birmingham Award” to go alongside graduates’ degree certificate.

The aim, according to Longworth is to “encourage students to think reflectively about their employability, their CV, their learning profile, that they are building through their degree right from day one through to the end”.

Those changes will also help assure parents who themselves studied humanities or similar subjects but are still worried about the implications.

“I’ve regularly spoken with families who say, we really support X’s ambition to do history or similar but what’s the reality of the career options? And then we can actually show them perhaps the reality rather than some of the perceptions,” she says.

Physically the university has also changed, after completing a rebuilding programme lasting a decade. The campus has shed the architecture of the 1960s and 1970s and restored its original horseshoe shape around a wide swathe of grass, trees and walkways leading to the university’s landmark clocktower, nicknamed Old Joe.

Jo Kite, the university’s director of external relations, says the redevelopment has created a new centre for the campus. “We call it the green heart, and it has absolutely animated the campus. That’s where we have our big community events, that’s where our graduation ball takes place.

“It really is a kind of beating heart, a lively space, and it’s moved a lot of people and events outdoors. At revision time, even well before exams, every bit of grass is covered with students when the sun shines.”

It wasn’t in relation to university that I first came across the organisation Rethink Repayment, which campaigns for a fairer settlement on student debt. I was looking into the astronomical numbers of young people who still live with their parents. It’s now more than a third of young men and more than a fifth of young women, statistics that get even crunchier when you realise that “young” describes anyone under 35.

There were various reasons – some had gone home after a health crisis, some really liked their parents, some were battling unemployment, but the single unifying theme was student debt. Those on incomes too low to start repaying couldn’t make rent; those in the lower repayment bracket (an annual income of £25,000 or thereabouts, depending on your loan plan) still couldn’t make rent, because they were spending 9% of their income repaying. And those on more than £50,000 were keeping less than 50p in every pound they earn because of their marginal tax rate. It’s always been sold to students when they take on this debt that it won’t count against their mortgage raising capacity, which technically it won’t – but any affordability check by a mortgage company or letting agent will factor in the monthly repayments.

It feels tactless to bring this up, just as a fresh wave of students heads off, with bigger, more exciting things on their minds than long-term debt. Yet it also feels remiss not to mention the fact that they’re being absolutely had. Florence, 29, who works as a solicitor in commercial litigation, is still living at home. She told me: “A lot of the time I’m reviewing contracts, and saying: ‘This is enforceable, sue them.’ The holes in what we were told are shocking. If student loans had come from an institutional lender, we would have a class action lawsuit.”

Without lingering on the unedifying details, such as how we’re all feeling about Nick Clegg nowadays, a quick recap on what the debate around student fees looked like when they were first hiked to £9,000 in 2012. There was a lot of anxiety about whether the government would ever get its money back, or whether a huge amount of this debt would have to be written off – what we didn’t factor in back then was that, this being the government, they could make the rules. If they wanted the interest on student loans to be set at the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation, plus up to 3%, they could simply snap their fingers and make it so. We talked a lot, too, about what those capped fees meant for universities – 10 years ago, £9,000 wasn’t enough for some courses but it was more than they needed for “classroom subjects” (a lot of humanities), which could then cross-subsidise. Now, with fees only increased to £9,790 in more than a decade, they often don’t even cover humanities courses – so worries about the sheer viability of what was previously one of the nation’s most successful sectors were well founded.

The students themselves were almost a side issue in this debate: the promise was that the debt would be more than offset by their increased earning capacity, once they had a degree, and, anyway, wouldn’t affect them until they could well afford it. This has turned out to be wildly untrue. Graduates are leaving with an average burden of £53,000, four or five times what it was in 2009, and the interest rates mean they can spend years repaying without making a dent in that amount. Graduate vacancies, meanwhile, were down 45% in August, compared with the same month last year, which is casually blamed on AI wiping out entry level jobs. Responsibility would be better situated with employers, who are choosing short-term cost-saving over their duty to their own companies, their society and the future.

It’s one thing to deprioritise the younger generation, it’s another to straight up scam them. I don’t want to tell any political party its business, but the one that makes a better offer than “pretend the problem doesn’t exist” stands to make enormous headway, and not just with the under-35s.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

title: Judge Blocks Controversial International Student Restrictions
summary:
Judge Blocks Controversial International Student Restrictions Johanna Alonso Mon, 09/14/2026 - 06:20 PM A Massachusetts judge issued the injunction hours before the regulation was set to take effect. Institutions worried it would harm international students. Byline(s) Johanna Alonso Judge Blocks Controversial International Student Restrictions
Johanna Alonso Mon, 09/14/2026 - 06:20 PM

A Massachusetts judge issued the injunction hours before the regulation was set to take effect. Institutions worried it would harm international students.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
The Department of Homeland Security’s widely criticized rule limiting how long international students can stay in the country won’t take effect Sept. 15 after a federal judge postponed the rule as part of a lawsuit challenging the policy.

Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts wrote in a 48-page order that Trump officials didn’t respond adequately to public comments on the rule or consider alternative options, among other violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, which governs how departments create regulations. The department also failed to show a rational connection between the rule and its purported national security objectives.

“The government’s contention that the rule is necessary to safeguard national security borders on the absurd,” Saylor wrote in the memorandum released Monday night. “It is based almost entirely on a small handful of anecdotes, each of which involved incidents that the new rule would do nothing to prevent or even mitigate.”

Finalized in July, the rule ends a nearly 50-year policy allowing international students in good academic standing to stay in the U.S. until they complete their studies, and instead limits them to four years. At that point, students could request an extension to stay, but it’s unclear how that process will work.

The lawsuit, filed weeks ago by eight organizations that primarily represent the higher education sector, seeks to vacate the rule, so Monday's order is just an initial step in the litigation. The DHS rule also applied to those with J-1 visas, which covers a range of cultural exchange programs, such as Fulbright scholars and foreign journalists who report in the U.S.

DHS has said the goal of the regulation is to improve national security and lower the number of students who stay in the country too long. The first Trump administration also attempted to make the same policy change, but it was never finalized.

Both international education advocates and institutions have raised the alarm about the regulation, which sparked 22,000 public comments—most of which opposed the rule. They’ve argued that the regulation will negatively impact a variety of students who need longer than four years to complete their programs, especially Ph.D. students, whose programs often take five or more years, in most cases. They also raised concerns that the regulation will make a U.S. education less appealing to international students, which will have ricochet effects on enrollment and revenue.

A group of more than a dozen institutions filed declarations explaining how the regulation was causing irreparable harm before it had even begun in hopes that the judge would stop the ruling from taking effect on Sept. 15.

Saylor wrote multiple times that DHS had no response to the plaintiffs’ arguments. He also referred to the regulation as “misguided,” “ill-advised,” “questionable,” and damaging to the United States, but noted that the injunction is not based on those judgements: “The role of the judiciary is not to ensure that the executive branch does not make unwise decisions.”

Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, one of the plaintiffs, told Inside Higher Ed in an email that she is grateful the decision “recognizes the serious and irreparable harm this rule would cause” and “preserves the longstanding system that enables our colleges and universities—and our country—to attract, educate and retain global talent.”

A status conference will be held Oct. 2.

title: Why We Haven’t Measured College-Level Learning
summary:
Why We Haven’t Measured College-Level Learning Doug Lederman Mon, 09/14/2026 - 03:00 AM Past efforts have failed because of tension over whether they’re for us (colleges) or them (our overseers). Let’s try again so colleges can prove they’re giving students what we promise them. Byline(s) Doug Lederman Why We Haven’t Measured College-Level Learning
Doug Lederman Mon, 09/14/2026 - 03:00 AM

Past efforts have failed because of tension over whether they’re for us (colleges) or them (our overseers). Let’s try again so colleges can prove they’re giving students what we promise them.

Byline(s)
Doug Lederman
full_text:
Two weeks ago in this space, I made a case that this vulnerable moment for higher education—of diminishing public confidence, financial strain, political attack and more—demands that colleges and universities show their value in part by proving that they’re actually enabling learning on their campuses.

I heard from a wide range of people, some agreeing and others sharpening their pitchforks. This is contested terrain: Some people who work in higher education just don’t like to be asked to prove themselves. Others worry (understandably given the history) that trying to “measure” whether and how much students learn might be reductive and produce endless administrative busywork.

I’ll soon respond here to the good questions some of you have raised since my original post. But first I want to finish what I started.

In the next couple of weeks, I’ll explain why we’ve historically tried (and failed) to measure learning and the importance of doing so now. Provide my early, and undoubtedly imperfect, ideas about how we might do that. And, importantly, distinguish what I’m envisioning from the accreditation- and accountability-driven “assessment” that a lot of you (not wrongly) view as the devil.

Today’s column offers my best attempt to explain how we ended up here: lacking, as I argued previously, “tangible, direct and incontrovertible proof that colleges and universities actually help learners develop the capabilities, skills and habits of mind that the institutions purport to deliver.”

Colleges and universities have long taken steps to understand whether students were learning, though in differing ways to suit different needs and satisfy different audiences.

For their own internal purposes, institutions tracked students’ progress toward a degree, largely through a process involving faculty development of a curriculum, student exposure to that curriculum measured in credit hours or “seat time,” a set of assignments and assessments graded by faculty experts deemed best able to judge whether students were learning, and a diploma backed up by a transcript with little detail.

For decades, most employers and Americans seemed to take on faith that people with a degree had learned enough or otherwise derived enough value to be “worth it.” That’s if they even thought about it; for many it was just assumed.

Institutions used also assessments for other “internal” purposes: to evaluate professors’ performance for tenure and promotion purposes; to “improve” courses and programs, understanding what works and doesn’t, and where students go off track; and to help instructors and designers rethink teaching practices and revise the curriculum as a result.

Those efforts aimed at institutional improvement had quite a bit of internal buy-in (since people tend to support things they’ve had a hand in creating); the central theme of Scott Gelber’s 2020 book, Grading the College: A History of Evaluating Teaching and Learning (Johns Hopkins University Press), he says, is that “when people come up with their own methods of evaluation, they have more faith in the validity” than in approaches imposed on them from outside.

But the internal methods lacked any currency outside the college (or even academic department) in question. And at various points in time, when questions arose about higher education’s quality or effectiveness, researchers, policy makers or politicians pressed for different kinds of learning assessment that might offer more comparability across institutions.

The first big push occurred in the mid-1980s, in the form of the 1984 report of the Study Group on the Conditions of Excellence in American Higher Education, which followed closely on the heels of the “Nation at Risk” report that spurred decades of K–12 reform.

The study group, which was commissioned by a unit in the then-new U.S. Department of Education but made up of prominent academics, recommended that colleges define educational excellence in terms of measurable student “outcomes” (knowledge, capacities and skills) rather than “inputs” such as the academic credentials of incoming students.

It also called on accreditors to hold colleges accountable for defining expectations, assessing whether students were meeting those expectations and developing systems for improving teaching and curricula based on those assessments.

Peter T. Ewell, who’s been called the “dean of the outcomes assessment movement in higher education,” cites this moment as the birth of that movement, and notes that it was plagued from the start by the dual purposes laid out by the study group—for internal improvement and for external accountability. (One of my all-time favorite op-eds in Inside Higher Ed was titled “Assessment for Us and Assessment for Them.”) Proponents’ desire to use the data to improve teaching and learning was increasingly greeted with skepticism from professors who believed the information would be “ritualistic” and potentially used against them in the court of tenure.

That tension escalated two decades later when then–Education Secretary Margaret Spellings’s Commission on the Future of Higher Education built its often-harsh critique partly around the idea that colleges and universities should define and measure “student learning outcomes” and that accreditors should police their work to ensure quality.

While Sen. Lamar Alexander blocked Spellings from taking formal action to force accreditors to set minimum levels of performance for student learning, colleges and accreditors alike got the message that, as the former college president and policy maker Jamienne Studley recalls, “if we didn’t do it ourselves, they would do it to us.” Even a self-described “curmudgeonly old classicist” like W. Robert Connor, then head of the Teagle Foundation, believed the time had come to measure learning more vigorously.

The threat of government-imposed requirements spawned a slew of initiatives over the next decade.

Some, like the Collegiate Learning Assessment, which was championed by the Spellings Commission, were standardized exams that sought to measure students’ critical thinking, analytic reasoning and written communication skills through a series of “performance tasks” and “writing prompts.” The CLA was notable because it was designed to measure how much learners grew over time, by comparing how students performed at the beginning and end of college. (The CLA’s embrace by the Spellings panel may have helped doom it.)

Many other advocates for stronger assessment focused not on standardized exams but on assessing portfolios of actual student work to find evidence of learning growth. The American Association of Colleges and Universities’ Valid Assessment of Learning in Undergraduate Education (VALUE) designed a set of rubrics to define 16 broad learning outcomes, applied the rubrics to samples of student work produced in courses and programs, and scored it. The now-defunct Multi-State Collaborative to Advance Quality Student Learning tried to do this at scale; hundreds of campuses still use VALUE in some way.

Still others intent on assessing student learning embraced competency-based education, an effort to recognize mastery of skills and knowledge without regard to how much time a learner spends in a program.

But none of these efforts fully took hold. Richard Arum, whose 2011 book Academically Adrift used data from experiments with the Collegiate Learning Assessment to argue that shockingly little learning was happening at many colleges, says there has been “no systematic investment in the use of these tools, let alone further development of them.”

He’s unsurprised that most colleges didn’t show much interest in measuring whether their students are learning—“that’s just basic self-interest” in not wanting to be held accountable. But Arum is disappointed that funders and research organizations haven’t pushed harder.

(Important side note: The colleges and universities that typically “lead” in higher education—the most visible institutions that are also often the wealthiest and most selective—have the least incentive to measure learning. The public already assumes they’re the “best,” so any mechanism that showed us which colleges actually helped their students grow the most might well diminish the “elites’” status rather than improve it.)

Meanwhile, the fears of many faculty members—that institutions and accreditors would adopt a top-down assessment strategy that purports to gauge whether students are learning but mostly creates box-checking busywork—has come to pass.

Rank-and-file faculty members (who, let’s be honest, will complain about anything they don’t see as being primarily in their interests) aren’t the only ones who think so: At one accreditor’s conference I covered in 2019, a researcher who has dedicated her life’s work to assessing student learning called the state of the field a “hot mess.”

“We had a round of assessment that was really detrimental, incredibly measurement focused,” she said.

What has happened to learning in the meantime? The whole point of this series of columns is that we don’t really know, but most of the few indicators we have suggest that the quality and quantity of learning aren’t going in the right direction. The latest measures of adult literacy and numeracy in the United States show declines, and while the most prominent studies finding declining academic workloads for college students are 15 years old, anecdotal evidence aplenty suggests that professors are assigning less reading and writing and students themselves are doing less work.

All while college grades have risen unabated: The best available (read: imperfect) evidence we have, from the Education Department’s National Postsecondary Student Aid Study, suggests that the average college grade point average rose from about 2.7 in the late 1980s to roughly 3.15 today. That’s widely interpreted as evidence of grade inflation rather than actual improvement, because students’ performance on standardized measures like the ACT and national exams like the National Assessment of Educational Progress have declined at the same time.

You know what’s also increased during this time? Public doubt about the value of higher education and of degrees. Is that because people doubt that learning is happening? That’s not a reason they tend to cite. But they are questioning whether graduates are prepared for employment and whether the time they spend at our institutions will help them enough to be worth what it costs.

Is learning the only piece of that? Of course not, which is why I’ve argued previously for a “broadly framed but very specific menu of indicators that would present a fuller picture of whether colleges and universities are delivering on the promises they make to students and to society more broadly.”

Learning should be at the center of that, though. I’m not talking about measuring it for either of the two historical reasons for assessment—“improvement” or “accountability”—but for a third purpose: “assessment to prove value.”

To prove to students and families and to employers (and maybe to ourselves?) that our colleges are actually delivering to learners what our mission statements say. That we have an actual plan for what we want them to know and be able to do after undertaking a set of learning experiences at our institutions, that we and they understand what that is, and that we’re committed to showing them they’re actually getting what we’ve promised.

I’ll save my working vision of what that might look like for the third and last piece of this series later this month. But at a high level, we would:

Define much more clearly (and ideally coherently, at an institutional or even cross-institutional level) the main capabilities, habits of mind and behaviors) we think a learner ought to develop (for me, it would be some set of durable skills on which faculty members, employers and others can find common cause and language);

Commit to a goal of helping every learner who puts in the work develop competence (if not mastery) of those capabilities;

Figure out some way (or ways) to measure students’ development of them so we (and they) can know how we’re all doing; and

Sounds simple, right?

title: EC English closes all global schools
summary:
EC English Language Centres has confirmed it is closing all its 25 language schools across seven destinations, effective immediately.

The post EC English closes all global schools  appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
In a statement released today, EC English CEO Andrew Mangion said English teaching and the company’s trading would cease with immediate effect, as of September 14, with a skeleton staff available tomorrow.

“We recognise that this is extremely difficult and disappointing news for you and your students,” Mangion wrote to partners.

“We understand the trust that you place in EC when recommending us to your students, and we are deeply sorry for the uncertainty and disruption that this decision will cause.”

The company told agents it was “genuinely sorry for the difficult conversations” they will now have to have with students and families with existing travel and accommodation arrangements.

In a public statement today, EC English announced it was commencing formal insolvency following “challenging financial conditions and the failure to secure additional investment”. It said it was with “profound sadness” that the group had reached this point.

The news follows last week’s eleventh-hour correspondence informing agents that EC English schools would be unable to accept students due to enrol in courses this week.

The details of what support will be offered to current students enrolled across EC locations in the UK, Ireland, Canada, USA, UAE, South Africa and Malta where it was originally founded, remain unknown.

But the company is understood to be working with sector bodies “to establish possible relocation options to alternative schools” and has vowed to share further information as soon as it is able.

In the UK, English UK has activated its Student Emergency Support (SES) scheme to help around 370 students currently enrolled at EC English’s four UK schools in London, Cambridge, Brighton and Manchester find replacement courses at other member centres, at no extra cost.

Jodie Gray, chief executive of English UK, said the organisation’s “immediate priority” was supporting affected students and helping them continue their studies “with as little disruption as possible”.

“We’re grateful for the offers of support from English UK member centres across the country and for how our community is pulling together,” said Gray. “By coordinating the response centrally, we ensure students are matched with suitable placements in a fair, orderly and effective way.”

English UK said students currently studying at EC’s UK schools would be contacted directly with information about replacement courses and next steps, with staff also available at all four centres on Tuesday September 15.

“EC English has been open for 35 years, and to see such an important world player close doors is a sad day for everyone,” Languages Canada executive director Gonzalo Peralta told The PIE News.

He said the 375 students currently enrolled in EC’s Toronto and Vancouver schools would be placed by Languages Canada in alternative programs to complete their study, with priority given to students completing their courses in the next two weeks.

Over 25 Languages Canada member schools have already offered to receive displaced students, with other offers coming in, said Peralta.

At its peak in 2019, EC English welcomed up to 50,000 students annually through its adult and junior programs.

We recognise that this is extremely difficult and disappointing news for you and your students

EC English Language Centres

For students currently in EC accommodation, the company has said it will continue to provide accommodation and support for existing students until September 19 “while arrangements are made for their onward travel or return home”.

Meanwhile, Mangion paid tribute to the “thousands” of employees who have contributed to building EC from a single school in Malta to an internationally recognised education organisation.

“EC has been much more than a business to those of us who have built it and worked within it. It has been a community of extraordinary people united by a belief in the power of education to bring people and cultures together.”

“Our team worked incredibly hard to build and sustain this company,” Mangion continued, recognising the “enormous efforts” of shareholders, employers, partners and advisers.

In a statement published earlier today (September 14), English UK said it would begin coordinating student support immediately if EC’s closure was confirmed.

This would include the possible continuation of programs at other accredited language centres without additional fees, and emergency accommodation support, where needed.

It said other providers had already offered to help, reflecting “the strength and care of the English UK community”.

Since the pandemic, the global English Language Teaching (ELT) sector has continued to face severe headwinds and sustained drops in student numbers, with experts warning the lower levels reflect a new sector structure rather than temporary decline.

Meanwhile, In South Africa, English South Africa (ESA) said it is coordinating with member schools to support affected students and agents, with a number of schools already indicating they are able to assist with transfers and alternative study arrangements. The schools include Avenue English, Bayswater, ELC (University of Cape Town), Good Hope Studies, LAL and IH Cape Town.

ESA said its immediate priority was to minimise disruption to students’ studies and help those who had chosen South Africa as their study destination continue their programs wherever possible.

“This is a very difficult moment for the sector globally, a sector that was so hard hit first by COVID and then, in many top destinations, by politics and policies that are the antithesis of what language education stands for,” said Peralta.

He added that Languages Canada was “pushing hard” to influence policies to change the tide of the sector in Canada, but that the immediate priority was supporting EC students.

title: Beyond the classroom: how international experiences shape future leaders
summary:
Junior international programs give young people the opportunity to experience a new country, discover new cultures, build meaningful friendships and, perhaps most importantly, discover what they are capable of.

The post Beyond the classroom: how international experiences shape future leaders appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Every summer, we welcome students from around the world to our junior programs in Canada and Australia. They may come to improve their English or French and experience another country, but after years of working with junior students, I believe what they take home goes much further.

A well-designed junior program creates a safe environment for young people to step outside their comfort zones. For some, it may be their first time away from their families, living in a residence or staying with a homestay family. For others, something as simple as learning to navigate a new city by public transit may be a completely new experience.

Through these everyday challenges, they become more confident, independent, and resourceful. This is also where leadership begins.

At this age, leadership does not necessarily mean being the person in charge. It can mean having the confidence to make a decision, finding a solution when something does not go as planned, contributing to a team or supporting a new friend who may be feeling unsure.

I saw these skills develop firsthand through ILSC Language Schools’ junior leadership program in Canada. International students experienced Canadian professional and academic life through visits to a local business, one of Canada’s leading universities and sessions with guest speakers.

Working independently and as a team, they applied their learning in real-world settings. The program culminated in a final project where students brought their learning together, highlighting their problem-solving skills, creativity, and innovation.

Experiences like these allow young people to see what they are capable of and develop the confidence to become future leaders.

But most of the important learning happens naturally through the international experience itself. When young people from different parts of the world live, learn, and explore together, they experience other cultures in a very personal way. They share meals, explore a new city together, laugh together, and discover both their differences and how much they have in common.

We see how transformative these experiences can be. After one student completed our junior program in Australia, her father wrote that they had discovered “a new girl,” someone “more confident, full of joy” and with her “head filled with dreams.”

He credited the experience of another culture, the care of her homestay family and the freedom she was given “to discover herself.”

His words capture how an international experience can change how a young person sees themselves and begin to recognize their own potential.

As national director of ILSC Language Schools’ junior programs in Canada, one of my favourite parts of every summer is watching this transformation happen. Students arrive in a new city, sometimes nervous and unsure of what to expect. Some are away from their families for the first time, hesitant to speak English or French or simply wondering whether they will make friends.

Then, little by little, you see the change. They become more comfortable speaking up, making decisions and looking out for one another. Most importantly, they form friendships with young people from around the world and learn about new cultures through those friendships.

By the end of the program, the goodbyes are always bittersweet. The same students who arrived not knowing what to expect are hugging new friends and activity leaders, exchanging contact information and often crying because they do not want the experience to end.

Those moments are incredibly heartwarming. I have had the privilege of watching their journey from beginning to end. They return home with greater independence, new friendships, unforgettable memories and, hopefully, a little more belief in what they are capable of.

For me, that is one of the greatest privileges of working in junior international education.

About the author: Vanessa Bhola, national director, juniors & corporate, ILSC Language Schools Canada, part of ILSC Education Group

Vanessa oversees ILSC Language Schools’ junior and family programs across Montréal, Toronto, and Vancouver, including language, leadership, and cultural immersion experiences in homestay and university residence settings. She is passionate about creating programs where international students feel welcomed and supported, while developing confidence, independence, and leadership skills through meaningful experiences and connections with others.

title: NTFS 2026: Empowering researchers to shape learning
summary: The post NTFS 2026: Empowering researchers to shape learning appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
New National Teaching Fellow, Dr Saneeya Qureshi, Head of Researcher Development and Culture at University of Liverpool, reflects on researcher education, learner agency and why teaching excellence begins with empowering others.

Working across cultures, disciplines and the space between research and education taught me that our greatest responsibility as educators is not simply to share knowledge, but to create the capacity and confidence for others to recognise their own agency.

This has arisen from my own experiences of navigating unfamiliar systems, questioning whether I belonged, and discovering that someone else’s belief in my potential could change everything. After reading my first MA Education assignment, Professor Richard Rose – then-module leader and later my exemplary PhD Supervisor – told me I should consider doctorate study and that he would find the funding to make it possible. His belief in my potential changed the direction of my career and my life. That experience has strengthened my determination to create educational environments where others experience that same sense of possibility.

What the Fellowship means to me

For me, receiving a National Teaching Fellowship recognises the importance of researcher education as an essential part of higher education. Many of the learners I work with would not instinctively describe themselves as educators: they are postgraduate researchers, research staff, supervisors, mentors and professional colleagues. Yet every day they teach, guide, challenge and inspire others.

When researchers are supported to become confident educators, supervisors and mentors, they are better equipped to create research environments in which people feel valued, able to contribute and empowered to develop others.

The Fellowship therefore shines a light not only on my work, but also on a community whose educational contribution is often overlooked, despite shaping thousands of learners every year.

What teaching excellence looks like

Growing up and working across Africa, Asia and Europe taught me that there is rarely a single way of understanding learning. Different cultures ask different questions, value different forms of knowledge and approach education in different ways. Rather than seeing these differences as barriers, I have learned to see them as opportunities. My intercultural perspective shapes how I design learning environments enabling different experiences to be recognised as strengths, learner voices to be genuinely valued and included, and researchers to develop the confidence to influence, and not simply participate in higher education. For me, teaching excellence is ultimately measured by what remains after we have left the room: greater confidence, stronger professional identities, deeper curiosity and the courage to contribute.

At the University of Liverpool, since 2017, I have worked to embed researcher education within research culture itself, helping establish institution-wide frameworks that integrate professional development, learning and teaching, supervision and leadership. Beyond Liverpool, I work with colleagues across Europe and beyond to strengthen mentoring, supervision and researcher development. I contribute to national and international policy and practice through organisations such as the European Educational Research Association, the Faraday Institution, the British Academy and Vitae.

Being a lifelong learner

One of the greatest insights in preparing my National Teaching Fellowship claim was not just reflections on past achievements, but on how I want to evolve as an educator and leader. It reminded me that my expertise should never become certainty and that curiosity is one of my greatest professional assets.

Those reflections reinforced something I had never articulated before: that my commitment to learner agency is not simply a pedagogic principle – it is a personal ethic rooted in my own experiences of marginalisation. That is why I continue to invest in learning, scholarship, mentorship, practice-sharing and why I regularly turn to colleagues whose perspectives push my thinking beyond familiar frameworks.

If I could offer one piece of advice to prospective National Teaching Fellows, it would be this: build your work around a question that refuses to leave you. Mine has always been: how can I help learners to recognise their own agency to teach, lead and shape the future of higher education?

Looking ahead

Educational change is rarely immediate, particularly when working across traditional boundaries. Not everyone will understand or share your commitment to lifelong learning, generous collaboration or practice-sharing. Work that challenges established boundaries or established ways of recognising educational contributions may not always be immediately understood or supported. Stay true to your values anyway. Keep learning and sharing generously with those who are open to improving their professional practice. Sustained and consistent impact speaks volumes.

Looking ahead, I intend to continue advocating for the recognition that researcher education takes many different forms and is shaped by diverse experiences, identities and professional journeys, including those, such as research technical professionals, whose educational contributions are frequently embedded within research practice and therefore less visible within traditional definitions of teaching.

This recognition is essential if we are to create the richest and most inclusive learning experiences for people at every stage of their development. Research, education and professional practice should never exist in isolation. When they are connected through generosity, curiosity and shared purpose, we create learning cultures in which everyone has the opportunity not simply to succeed, but to help others succeed too.

Dr Saneeya Qureshi is Head of Researcher Development and Culture, University of Liverpool. Recognised for advancing learner agency through researcher education, Dr Qureshi creates inclusive opportunities that empower researchers and educators to develop confidence, voice and professional identity. Working across policy, pedagogy and research culture, she strengthens the people, practices and systems that shape learning, teaching and research supervision internationally.

title: Jenseits des linearen Denkens: Sich selbst verbessernde KI als Herausforderung für eine zukunftsorientierte Hochschulbildung
summary:
Selbstverbessernde KI entwickelt sich mit hoher Geschwindigkeit und stellt die linearen Planungs- und Entscheidungslogiken von Hochschulen infrage. Wie können Hochschulen ihre Organisationsentwicklung anpassen, ohne dabei akademische Werte und menschliche Steuerung aus dem Blick zu verlieren?

The post Jenseits des linearen Denkens: Sich selbst verbessernde KI als Herausforderung für eine zukunftsorientierte Hochschulbildung appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
“The greatest shortcoming of the human race is our inability to understand the exponential function.”, so die Aussage des früheren US-amerikanischen Physikerprofessors Albert Allen Bartlett (1923-2013) bei seinen Vorträgen zu Arithmetic, Population and (Bartlett 1969). Er wollte damit auf die Gefahr hinweisen, dass dauerhaftes prozentuales Wachstum von Bevölkerung oder Ressourcenverbrauch, was durch eine Exponentialfunktion abgebildet wird, in einem endlichen System nicht unbegrenzt möglich ist.

Genau dieses Zitat hat der bekannte Bildungsinfluencer Daniel Jung im August 2026 in seinem Podcast-Talk „Exponentielles Wachstum: Kannst du es verstehen?“ mit dem Bonner Informatikprofessor Christian Bauckhage am Beispiel generativer KI und der zu beobachtenden Leistungssteigerung aufgegriffen (Jung 2026). Bis heute fällt es uns Menschen schwer, das exponentielle Wachstum mit seinen Auswirkungen zu begreifen und entsprechend zu handeln. In diese Kategorie fallen generative KI-Systeme, die sich selbst weiterentwickeln können. Sie scheinen unsere menschliche Vorstellungkraft zu sprengen und treffen auf den Bereich Bildung. Deren Institutionen gelten als strukturkonservativ, entwickeln sich in kleinen Schritten und denken traditionell sequenziell, d. h. linear: Curricula werden in Jahreszyklen fortgeschrieben, Kompetenzen schrittweise aufgebaut, Reformen inkrementell umgesetzt. Über Jahrzehnte erschien diese lineare Form der Organisationsentwicklung „passend“ und sorgte für Stabilität und Sicherheit für alle Beteiligten. In einer KI-Ära, in der generative KI-Systeme ihre Fähigkeiten in Monaten statt in Jahrzehnten in unvorhersehbarer Weise verändern, wird dieser planbasierte Ansatz zum Risiko. Wer technologische Entwicklung gedanklich als gleichmäßige Gerade in die Zukunft verlängert, unterschätzt systematisch sowohl das Tempo als auch die qualitativen Sprünge, die mit nichtlinearer Dynamik einhergehen.

Für den Bildungsbereich ist diese Fehleinschätzung besonders folgenreich. Sie kann entweder in Alarmismus und Aktionismus münden, sobald ein Entwicklungssprung sichtbar wird, oder in Untätigkeit unter der trügerischen Annahme, es bliebe noch genügend Zeit – oder noch schlimmer in Ignoranz und Resignation als Ausdruck von Überforderung. Diese Verhaltensweisen werden einer zukunftsorientierten Hochschulbildung nicht gerecht. In diesem Papier wird die Position vertreten, dass Hochschulen ihr lineares Denken in der Organisationsentwicklung, zugunsten einer schnelleren Adaptionsfähigkeit, überwinden müssen.

Ganz gegensätzlich zeigt sich die Haltung der Arizona State University als „Public Enterprise“, mit dem Anspruch einer „Learning Economy“, die der Organisationsentwicklung vieler deutscher Hochschulen diametral entgegensteht. Das skizzierte Tempo des Wandels signalisiert aber auch das ungelöste Problem der begrenzten menschlichen Anpassungsgeschwindigkeit, so wie in Abb. 1 dargestellt. Bereits heute spüren wir als Individuum vielfach die Überforderung des „Nicht-Mithaltens-Können“. Der Austausch und das kollektive Lernen in Netzwerken unter Ausnutzung von Synergien sind klassische Lösungsansätze, deren Potenziale nicht ausgeschöpft erscheinen, ohne dass sie die finale Lösung bieten.

Turing führte bereits 1948 eine frühe Diskussion über „modifiable“ und „self-modifying machinery“ deren Verhalten und gespeicherte Instruktionen durch interne Operationen verändert werden können (Turing 2004) . Knapp 20 Jahre später wurde die Idee einer sich selbst verbessernden KI 1965 von Goods vorgestellt (Good 1965). Seine Überlegung bezog sich auf eine ultraintelligente Maschine, die jeden Menschen in sämtlichen intellektuellen Tätigkeiten übertreffen und selbst noch intelligentere Maschinen entwickeln könnte. Dadurch entstünde eine sich selbst verstärkende „Intelligenzexplosion“, bei der die menschliche Intelligenz schnell zurückbliebe. Die erste ultraintelligente Maschine wäre somit möglicherweise „die letzte Erfindung, die der Mensch je machen muss“, allerdings unter der Voraussetzung, dass sie kontrollierbar bliebe und sich kooperativ verhalte.

Von Schmidhuber wurde 2003 (Schmidhuber 2003), inspiriert von Kurt Gödel’s berühmten selbstreferenziellen Formeln (1931), das Konzept der selbst-optimierenden Gödel-Maschine vorgestellt. Dabei handelt es sich um das theoretische Konzept eines Programms, das jeden Teil seines eigenen Programmcodes verändern kann, einschließlich des Mechanismus, mit dem es nach Verbesserungen sucht.

Über lange Zeit blieben solche Ansätze in der Theorie verhaftet, da sie auf formalen Beweisen beruhten und praktisch kaum umsetzbar waren. Aber seit 2025 weisen moderne KI-Agentensysteme den Weg in die Anwendung. Die Darwin-Gödel-Maschine von Sakana AI und Mitarbeitenden der University of British Columbia (Sakana AI 2025) überträgt Schmidhubers Konzept in einen darwinistisch-evolutionären, empirisch validierten Prozess: Ein Agent modifiziert seinen eigenen Code, erprobt Varianten und behält erfolgreiche Versionen in einem Archiv.

Diese Entwicklungen folgen einem sichtbaren Trend mit ambitionierten Zielsetzungen wie z. B. die von Richard Socher und seinem Start-up angestrebte rekursive Superintelligenz (Killian 2026). Dass es sich hierbei nicht länger um ein KI-Nischenthema handelt, zeigt nicht zuletzt der erste eigens diesem Thema gewidmete Workshop auf der ICLR 2026 (ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI with Recursive Self-Improvement 2026).

Auch radikale Ansätze treten vermehrt auf, beispielhaft seien das amerikanische Start-up DISCOVERY LOOP genannt mit der Zielsetzung, Forschung in einen skalierbaren, automatisierten und kontinuierlich lernenden Produktionsprozess zu verwandeln analog zu „self-driving labs“ (DISCOVERY LOOP 2026) oder das Start-up inherent labs (Inherent Laboratories 2026) aus London, das in seinem Manifest mit dem Titel: „Living within the Experiment“ diese Zielsetzung formuliert: „Die Verwirklichung dieser Zukunft bedeutet, auf eine radikale Form der rekursiven Selbstverbesserung zu setzen: eine, die sicher in einer gesamten Institution funktioniert“ (übersetzt aus dem Englischen).

Der damit einhergehende „Change“ trifft in den Hochschulen auf ein vielschichtiges Spannungsfeld. Einerseits eröffnen teilautonome Agentensysteme erhebliche Chancen: Sie können Forschungsprozesse beschleunigen (Ghareeb et al. 2026), Routineanalysen übernehmen und in der Lehre (Weßels 2025) als adaptive, dialogfähige Werkzeuge dienen. Andererseits stellen sie eine Herausforderung für historisch gewachsene akademische Praktiken und Werte dar. Die Nachvollziehbarkeit von Ergebnissen sinkt, wenn Systeme Hypothesen bilden, Experimente planen und auswerten, ohne dass der Weg offengelegt wird. Prüfungsprozesse und die wissenschaftliche Integrität geraten unter Druck, wenn Autorschaft und Eigenleistung in der Ko-Aktivität von Mensch und KI nicht präzise zugeordnet und bewertet werden können. Und die Kompetenzentwicklung der Studierenden ist scheinbar bedroht, wenn Denk-, Analyse- und Urteilsschritte delegiert werden, die als Kompetenzziele des Studiums angestrebt werden. Zentrale Ursache dieser artikulierten Sorgen und Bedenken sind unzureichende KI-Qualifizierungsmaßnahmen für Lehrende, „alte“ didaktische Konzepte, die KI vorrangig als Störfaktor sehen und fehlende lernförderliche Ansätze zur zeitgemäßen Integration von KI in die Lehre und das Lernen unter Berücksichtigung der KI-induzierten Kompetenzverschiebungen (Weßels und Maibaum 2026).

Sich selbst verbessernde KI hat heute weder den Rang der Superintelligenz erreicht, noch darf sie als irrelevanter Hype fehlinterpretiert werden, den die Hochschulbildung ignorieren darf. Hochschulen, die auf festgefahrenen Wegen nur in kleinen Schritten nach vorne gehen, werden den veränderten Rahmenbedingungen und der Lebensrealität insbesondere der Studierenden in der agentischen Ära nicht mehr gerecht. Die Arizona State University zeigt, dass Anpassungsfähigkeit die Attraktivität bei Studienbewerber:innen erhöhen und daher als Wettbewerbsvorteil betrachtet werden kann.

Gleichzeitig muss die Management-Ebene einer Hochschule ihren Führungsaufgaben gerecht werden und die Organisationsmitglieder auf diesem Entwicklungsprozess, der von vielen Ängsten geprägt ist, unterstützen und begleiten. Dass der KI-Einsatz auch als Lösungsansatz für KI-induzierte Herausforderungen eingesetzt werden kann, zeigt eine vorbildliche Umsetzungsinitiative der Technischen Hochschule Brandenburg mit einer Stellenausschreibung für die Entwicklung eines KI-basierten Curriculumsmanagement (Technische Hochschule Brandenburg 2026).

Eine zukunftsorientierte Hochschulbildung benötigt die Offenheit und Bereitschaft, sich radikalen und als sprunghaft empfundenen Veränderungsprozessen zu unterziehen. Die Zielsetzung ist klar: Es geht darum, die Chancen der Technologie bestmöglich zu nutzen, flexible Räume für Wachstum und Veränderung zu schaffen und zugleich den Geist akademischer Bildung und den Anspruch auf überprüfbaren Erkenntnisgewinn zu bewahren.

Diese Entwicklungen folgen einem sichtbaren Trend mit ambitionierten Zielsetzungen wie z. B. die von Richard Socher und seinem Start-up angestrebte rekursive Superintelligenz (Killian 2026). Dass es sich hierbei nicht länger um ein KI-Nischenthema handelt, zeigt nicht zuletzt der erste eigens diesem Thema gewidmete Workshop auf der ICLR 2026 (ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI with Recursive Self-Improvement 2026).

Auch radikale Ansätze treten vermehrt auf, beispielhaft seien das amerikanische Start-up DISCOVERY LOOP genannt mit der Zielsetzung, Forschung in einen skalierbaren, automatisierten und kontinuierlich lernenden Produktionsprozess zu verwandeln analog zu „self-driving labs“ (DISCOVERY LOOP 2026) oder das Start-up inherent labs (Inherent Laboratories 2026) aus London, das in seinem Manifest mit dem Titel: „Living within the Experiment“ diese Zielsetzung formuliert: „Die Verwirklichung dieser Zukunft bedeutet, auf eine radikale Form der rekursiven Selbstverbesserung zu setzen: eine, die sicher in einer gesamten Institution funktioniert“ (übersetzt aus dem Englischen).

Der damit einhergehende „Change“ trifft in den Hochschulen auf ein vielschichtiges Spannungsfeld. Einerseits eröffnen teilautonome Agentensysteme erhebliche Chancen: Sie können Forschungsprozesse beschleunigen (Ghareeb et al. 2026), Routineanalysen übernehmen und in der Lehre (Weßels 2025) als adaptive, dialogfähige Werkzeuge dienen. Andererseits stellen sie eine Herausforderung für historisch gewachsene akademische Praktiken und Werte dar. Die Nachvollziehbarkeit von Ergebnissen sinkt, wenn Systeme Hypothesen bilden, Experimente planen und auswerten, ohne dass der Weg offengelegt wird. Prüfungsprozesse und die wissenschaftliche Integrität geraten unter Druck, wenn Autorschaft und Eigenleistung in der Ko-Aktivität von Mensch und KI nicht präzise zugeordnet und bewertet werden können. Und die Kompetenzentwicklung der Studierenden ist scheinbar bedroht, wenn Denk-, Analyse- und Urteilsschritte delegiert werden, die als Kompetenzziele des Studiums angestrebt werden. Zentrale Ursache dieser artikulierten Sorgen und Bedenken sind unzureichende KI-Qualifizierungsmaßnahmen für Lehrende, „alte“ didaktische Konzepte, die KI vorrangig als Störfaktor sehen und fehlende lernförderliche Ansätze zur zeitgemäßen Integration von KI in die Lehre und das Lernen unter Berücksichtigung der KI-induzierten Kompetenzverschiebungen (Weßels und Maibaum 2026).

Sich selbst verbessernde KI hat heute weder den Rang der Superintelligenz erreicht, noch darf sie als irrelevanter Hype fehlinterpretiert werden, den die Hochschulbildung ignorieren darf. Hochschulen, die auf festgefahrenen Wegen nur in kleinen Schritten nach vorne gehen, werden den veränderten Rahmenbedingungen und der Lebensrealität insbesondere der Studierenden in der agentischen Ära nicht mehr gerecht. Die Arizona State University zeigt, dass Anpassungsfähigkeit die Attraktivität bei Studienbewerber:innen erhöhen und daher als Wettbewerbsvorteil betrachtet werden kann.

Gleichzeitig muss die Management-Ebene einer Hochschule ihren Führungsaufgaben gerecht werden und die Organisationsmitglieder auf diesem Entwicklungsprozess, der von vielen Ängsten geprägt ist, unterstützen und begleiten. Dass der KI-Einsatz auch als Lösungsansatz für KI-induzierte Herausforderungen eingesetzt werden kann, zeigt eine vorbildliche Umsetzungsinitiative der Technischen Hochschule Brandenburg mit einer Stellenausschreibung für die Entwicklung eines KI-basierten Curriculumsmanagement (Technische Hochschule Brandenburg 2026).

Eine zukunftsorientierte Hochschulbildung benötigt die Offenheit und Bereitschaft, sich radikalen und als sprunghaft empfundenen Veränderungsprozessen zu unterziehen. Die Zielsetzung ist klar: Es geht darum, die Chancen der Technologie bestmöglich zu nutzen, flexible Räume für Wachstum und Veränderung zu schaffen und zugleich den Geist akademischer Bildung und den Anspruch auf überprüfbaren Erkenntnisgewinn zu bewahren.

title: Norma senza presidio: l’università pubblica e il paradosso della didattica digitale
summary: Con la chiusura dei fondi PNRR per i Digital Education Hub, il sistema pubblico ha prodotto contenuti, competenze e professionalità nella didattica digitale, ma resta fuori dal canale in cui la domanda cresce.
